data.title: Alito: Overturning Roe v. Wade took 'courage' from Supreme Court justices
data.description:
Justice Samuel Alito said his vote to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022 alongside the Supreme Court’s six conservative justices, took “courage.”

In a preview for his interview with CBS News, Alito was asked if there was a particular decision that took courage.

“Well, the leading example is Dobbs [v. Jackson]. I think that required courage by all of the justices in the majority,” he said. “We didn’t know it at the time. We didn’t know it when we produced the draft that was leaked, but it required courage to go ahead with that because of the implications.”

“There are others. I mean, there are cases that have resulted in the loss of old friendships, that’s something that you have to live with,” Alito continued.

When asked if part of the job of a Supreme Court Justice is to lose friends, receive death threats or wear a bulletproof vest, he responded, “it’s part of the job that you’re going to displease people by making decisions on controversial matters because one side or the other is going to really dislike you because of the decisions.”

“The physical threats and the harassment represent something new in our society and something that’s quite disturbing, and I think it’s a danger,” Alito concluded. 

Over four years ago, the Supreme Court eliminated the nearly 50-year-old constitutional right to abortion and handed states authority to drastically limit or ban the procedure. 

Alito wrote in the majority opinion — which was leaked a month before it was unveiled — “Roe was egregiously wrong from the start,” adding that its precedent “had damaging consequences.”

The decision drew public outcry with protests outside the Supreme Court building in Washington, D.C. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said at the time the decision marked “one of the darkest days our country has ever seen.” 

An NBC poll from 2023 found 53 percent of Americans strongly disapprove of Roe v. Wade’s overturn. 

Since then, many states across the U.S. have enacted near total bans on access to abortion with limited exceptions and imposed penalties for health professionals who aid in providing access to the procedure.

The Big Story 

How did the beltway take Trump’s AI accord?

In a deep dive, The Hill’s Julia Shapero and Mallory Wilson examine how Trump’s “self-policing” AI accord is landing in Washington as concerns mount over the tech’s safety.

© Alex Brandon, Associated Press

While Trump says industry officials can self-police, critics argue AI needs more oversight to keep development from getting out of hand — even as some described the accord as a step in the right direction.

 

One expert told us the administration’s concerns may be “sincere,” but the pledge is not a “solution” to preventing the potential risks of AI development. 

 

Several of the biggest players in the industry signed the one-page document Tuesday, which included four “layers of controls and audits.”

 

It declares that AI companies should implement “robust” internal controls over models, empower an internal crew to crosscheck controls and mediate any issues, partner with external auditors to evaluate their controls and designate an independent committee of the board of directors to oversee reports from the operating teams.

 

Some lawmakers, including members of his own party, expressed skepticism over the accord.

 

Sen. Josh Halwey (R-Mo.) called it a “good step” but stopped short of saying lawmakers can take AI executives at their world.

SEC’s ‘crypto mom’ says adieu

© Andrew Harnik, AP

Hester Peirce, who became known as “crypto mom” at the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), is bidding the agency adieu.

 

The SEC commissioner, who departs Friday after eight years in the role, was a key advocate for the industry during a period that saw Washington’s views on digital assets shift wildly.

 

“Serving this great nation at the Securities and Exchange Commission has been the honor of my professional lifetime,” she wrote in her resignation letter, which she shared to social media last week.

 

“The United States is exceptional because its unifying thread is a commitment to liberty,” Peirce continued. “A nation that elevates freedom of thought, expression, and action unlocks the great potential of its people to meet one another’s needs.”

 

“That ethos runs through the American securities markets, where innovates meet retail and institutional investors so that together they can build a vibrant economy.”

 

Her departure leaves the SEC with just two commissioners, Chair Paul Atkins and Mark Uyeda. Both are Republican appointees.

 

The agency typically has a five-member bipartisan commission but has dwindled down over the past two years. 

 

Notably, the SEC issued a final rule Wednesday updating its quorum requirements. The new rule declares that one commissioner can constitute quorum if they are the only member who can participate.

The Big Story 

Marines exceed 2026 recruiting goals 

The U.S. Marines said they exceeded their fiscal year 2026 recruiting goals across every component and category, enlisting over 31,000 new recruits. 

U.S. Central Command via AP

The Marines brought in 31,250 new recruits, 1,672 officers and 3,503 prior-service reserve Marines in what the service branch called a “historic, department-wide rebound” in military enlistments.

 

“Our success this year is a testament to the disciplined execution of our elite recruiting force on the streets of America,” Marine Corps Maj. Gen. Walker M. Field, Marine Corps Recruiting Command commanding general, said in a statement on Thursday. 

 

“Likewise, it is emblematic of the legion of young Americans who are choosing, of their own volition, to serve this great nation of ours,” Field said. “The few young Americans who earn the title of Marine espouse the rare trifecta of physical, intellectual and moral fortitude to become elite warriors.”

 

While the Marines said the recruiting duty remains “challenging,” the 2026 landscape was the “most favorable” in the last five years, driven by “high” volume of interested applicants and “historically strong retention rates” across the Corps. 

 

Last year, the Marines recruited 30,536 active-duty and reserve enlisted Marines, just above 30,501 enlisted in 2024.

 

Other service branches all hit their recruiting goals for this year.

 

The Navy added 45,112 new sailors, while the Army brought in over 61,500 soldiers. 

 

The Air Force enlisted 31,950 airmen and 730 Space Force Guardians.

data.title: Kushner pushes back on CNN report about Israeli investments tied to military
data.description:
Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and U.S. special envoy, is pushing back on a CNN report alleging his private equity firm had ties to a company heavily involved in Israel’s military. 

“CNN published a deeply misleading story and headline suggesting that my diplomatic work in the Middle East somehow benefited investments in Israeli defense companies,” Kushner wrote on social media Friday.

The outlet identified Kushner-founded Affinity Partners as the largest stakeholder in Phoenix Financial — a company that reportedly invested at least $456 million into various firms involved with Israel’s ongoing military campaign in Gaza.

“Phoenix is not a defense company. It is one of Israel’s largest publicly traded financial institutions, highly regulated and managing approximately $220 billion across thousands of investments,” the special envoy continued, adding that the company is the “Israeli equivalent of Vanguard or Fidelity.”

“Affinity is an SEC-registered investment firm. Our investment in Phoenix is public and dates to before President Trump was re-elected and before I returned to public service. Affinity does not own the defense companies highlighted in CNN’s story.”

Kushner has served as a U.S. special envoy throughout Trump’s second term, becoming an instrumental figure in leading peace talks between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Hamas. He and Steve Witkoff have also headed negotiations related to the U.S. and Israel’s war in Iran, as well as Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Rep. Robert Garcia (R-Calif.) and Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) wrote a letter to the White House in March expressing “serious concerns” about Kushner’s potential “conflicts of interest” — saying they feared the president’s son-in-law would be allowed to leverage his political influence as a U.S. envoy for personal financial gain.

Kushner reportedly led meetings with Netanyahu and Hamas leadership in August, though a peace deal remains uncertain. The militant group has since demanded that Israeli forces halt their attacks on the Gaza Strip, withdraw from the region and hands over weapons — calls that Israel’s prime minister firmly rejected.

However, Hamas did agree to Trump’s Board of Peace 15-point roadmap in July, which outlined steps to a peace agreement, but the group reiterated that it would only follow its suggestions if Israel halted attacks. Netanyahu rejected the plan in a rare public show of defiance against the Trump administration, one of Israel’s closest allies.

Two days after Kushner reportedly asked Netanyahu to wind down attacks in the Gaza Strip, Israeli strikes killed at least 10 people, according to the Associated Press, citing local hospitals and the Palestinian Red Crescent. 

Kushner concluded his Friday statement saying the report “will not distract me from the work President Trump asked me to do: help end wars, bring people together and pursue peace.” He also echoed his father-in-law’s attacks against CNN, accusing its story on Kushner as being “misleading” and a “provocative headline.”

data.title: Ex-GOP lawmaker sentenced to 10 years in prison
data.description:
Former Florida Rep. David Rivera (R) was sentenced to 10 years in federal prison Friday for his undisclosed role in a multimillion-dollar lobbying campaign on behalf of the Venezuelan government under the first Trump administration. 

Rivera, a longtime friend and former roommate of Secretary of State Marco Rubio, has been in federal custody without bond since a Miami jury convicted him in May on charges of conspiracy to commit money laundering and other crimes connected to this $50 million lobbying scheme.

The campaign ran from 2017 to 2018, under ousted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro’s regime. Rivera was not serving in the House when he and his consultant, Esther Nuhfer, secretly lobbied U.S. lawmakers and members of the first Trump administration on behalf of PDV USA, the U.S. affiliate of Venezuela’s state-run oil company. 

The pair was found guilty of violating the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) after a weekslong trial, during which Rubio, Texas Rep. Pete Sessions (R) and a top Washington lobbyist testified. All asserted they were unaware of a contract between PDV USA and Rivera’s consulting company. 

Prosecutors alleged in an 11-page indictment unsealed in 2022 that Venezuela’s then-foreign minister, Delcy Rodríguez, recruited Rivera to try to convince the Trump administration to ease sanctions on the country. Rodríguez has served as the acting Venezuelan president since the US arrested Maduro in January.

President Trump opted not to loosen these restrictions, instead moving to sanction Maduro’s government in within his first six months in the White House.

The indictment also claimed Rivera and Nuhfer signed a contract to receive a total of $50 million from the scheme — broken up into five $5 million payments and one amounting to $25 million. The pair ultimately received about $20 million after the company terminated the contract, prosecutors said. 

Rivera’s attorneys argued that the defendants operated in good faith and were not required to disclose their work under FARA. The defense lawyers previously applied for a presidential pardon in June and plan to appeal this sentence, according to The Associated Press.

The Republican represented Florida’s 25th Congressional District in the House for one term from 2011 to 2013. He was fined $456,000 in 2021 following several state and federal investigations into his role in an improper campaign finance scheme.

His consultant was given a five-year prison sentence in August for her role in the illegal lobbying, the Miami Herald reported.

data.title: Judge halts contentious border construction in and near Texas's Big Bend national park
data.description:
A federal judge on Friday halted contentious Trump administration border construction plans in Texas’s Big Bend region. 

Judge Kathleen Cardone, a George W. Bush appointee, wrote that the administration can’t  “build border barrier or related infrastructure, or engage in any construction or ground disturbing activities” in the region.

“The Court finds that Plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits of at least one of the claims in suit, that there is a likelihood that they will suffer serious, irreparable harm without an injunction, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest weigh in their favor,” Cardone wrote. 

Border construction in the area has drawn criticism from Democrats and Republicans alike, who have warned of adverse effects on Big Bend National Park, the local economy and landowners who live near the border. Opponents of such construction have argued that the area’s rugged terrain forms a natural border.

Earlier this year, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem waived environmental laws to expedite the construction of barriers and roads across the Big Bend sector.

The administration has said it will not build a large border wall inside the national park, but is pursuing other construction activity there. It does still appear to be planning wall construction in other parts of the region, which sits along the bend of the Rio Grande.

The Hill has reached out to Customs and Border Protection and the Department of Homeland Security for comment on the judge’s order.

The order was celebrated by opponents of the construction.

“This is a historic victory for Big Bend and everyone who loves this wild corner of Texas,” said Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, in a written statement.

“No administration has the right to destroy a crown-jewel national park for political theatre. With a federal court ordering the bulldozers to stop, Big Bend gets to breathe. But this fight is far from over. We won’t rest until Big Bend’s environmental protections are fully restored and the illegal waiver that allowed so much destruction is gone for good,” Jordahl added.

data.title: Trump shrugs off South Korea's uncertainty on $54B Alaska energy investment
data.description:
President Trump brushed off questions Friday over whether he jumped the gun in announcing that South Korea would fund a natural gas pipeline in Alaska, which South Korean officials have said is still under discussion.

“Well, I didn’t jump the gun. I mean, they were there and they were represented,” Trump told reporters before departing the White House for a campaign stop. “If they don’t want to do it, that’s OK with me. I’ll just charge them more.”

“Tell them if they don’t sign shortly, I’m gonna double it up,” he added, apparently referring to tariffs.

The president announced Wednesday that South Korea would be investing up to $200 billion in energy projects across the U.S., including a long-planned liquified natural gas (LNG) pipeline in Alaska. It would also include eight nuclear power plants and a natural gas plant in Texas.

The deal came as part of a trade agreement between South Korea and the U.S. in which the U.S. would lower the tariff rate on South Korea to 15 percent. Trump said the investment from South Korea for the pipeline would be $54 billion.

But South Korean officials pushed back on the announcement.

South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, wrote on social media that the Alaska LNG project will proceed if its financial viability is confirmed and the project complies with South Korean legal procedures.

The Wall Street Journal also reported that South Korean Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said, “Putting out figures, or using definitive language, goes far beyond what was agreed.”

data.title: Trump says he's 'worried' about Whatley in North Carolina
data.description:
President Trump said he was worried about North Carolina GOP Senate nominee Michael Whatley’s election chances as the Senate Republican super PAC began canceling reservations in the state on Friday. 

“I think he’s a great man and I am worried about him,” Trump told reporters on the South Lawn en route to a campaign rally in Alabama. 

“I hope he wins. He was a great leader for the whole Republican Party when I won, and he’d be a great senator,” he continued. 

Trump’s comments come after the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC for Senate GOP leadership, canceled $6.5 million ad reservations in North Carolina on Friday. 

Polls show Whatley trailing his Democratic opponent, former Gov. Roy Cooper (D). 

A Catawba College and YouGov poll released this week showed Cooper with a 10-point lead over Whatley. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the race as “lean Democrat.”

Trump and Vice President Vance each traveled to North Carolina to campaign with Whatley last month.

data.title: Thousands of legal immigrants lose Medicaid coverage as 'big, beautiful' cuts begin
data.description:
Thousands of refugees and other legal immigrants lost their health coverage on Oct. 1, marking some of the first significant coverage losses under the Medicaid cuts in the GOP’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act. 

States and advocacy groups have been trying to warn immigrants who were previously eligible for Medicaid — such as refugees, asylees without a green card, survivors of domestic violence and victims of sex trafficking — that they no longer qualify.  

“This is a real shift that’s going to create a serious gap in access to healthcare services,” said Adriana Cadena, executive director of the Protecting Immigrant Families Coalition. “The folks who have survived the most trauma, whether it’s war, natural disaster, or sexual assault, are going to be the folks who are going to be losing coverage.” 

Advocates say the eligibility restrictions on immigrants will mean people lose access to doctors, as well as medications and treatments for diabetes and other chronic diseases. 

Providers will lose longtime patients, and hospitals expect a spike in uninsured emergency room visits, which could drive up health system costs. Hospitals are required to provide emergency care regardless of immigration status and are reimbursed by Emergency Medicaid.  

The law does not impact green card holders or a few other small groups of immigrants. The law also doesn’t change existing state options to cover children and pregnant immigrants; states can still receive federal matching funding for these populations. 

More to come

The Medicaid eligibility restrictions are merely the first in a host of provisions that are projected to strip away government-sponsored health coverage. 

Starting next year, more than 1 million immigrants are projected to lose Affordable Care Act plan subsidies as well as Medicare coverage. 

The changes are part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, President Trump and congressional Republicans’ signature domestic policy legislation that he signed into law with much fanfare in 2025. The law is projected to cut Medicaid spending by $900 billion through 2034, largely by imposing new eligibility restrictions, work requirements and cost sharing. 

In selling the bill to Congress, the administration argued that “illegal aliens” would be losing Medicaid.  

“The One, Big, Beautiful Bill is a generational chance to protect Medicaid for Americans by removing at least 1.4 million illegal immigrants from the program,” the White House said in a May 2025 statement.  

But immigrants without legal status are already ineligible for federally funded health coverage. 

The law also imposed restrictions on legal immigrants’ use of food stamps, Medicare and the Children’s Health Insurance Program. 

Major impact

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimated that the Medicaid changes would lead to roughly 100,000 lawfully present immigrants losing health insurance.  

Immigrant advocates said the actual number could be significantly higher because of the Trump administration’s slowing of green card applications; many legal immigrants will be kicked off Medicaid while they wait for their application decisions. 

According to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, it takes an average of 30 months to process an application for permanent residence from a refugee who was admitted more than a year ago. 

Ben D’Avanzo, senior strategist at the National Immigration Law Center, said it was “shocking” to see Republicans try to demonize immigrants who had been admitted to the country for humanitarian reasons. 

“These are people who are among the most vulnerable and among the most vetted categories of immigrants,” D’Avanzo said.  

Federal officials said the law ensures U.S. government money is spent on Americans, and forces immigrants to be self-sufficient.  

“Immigrants must be able to support themselves and not depend on benefits paid for by hard-working American taxpayers. President Trump and this administration will always put American citizens first,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement.  

Steven Camarota, the director of research at the Center for Immigration Studies, a think tank focused on lower immigration rates, said he supports the administration’s attempt to curtail immigrants’ use of welfare programs.  

But he said the savings from restricting immigrants from Medicaid are fairly modest. Much bigger savings would result from overhauling the entire immigration system  

“If we really want legal immigrants to use less welfare we would need to have a system that selects future immigrants based on skills who are unlikely to need welfare,’ Camarota said.   

Advocates said many of the people losing coverage will be forced to turn to emergency rooms for care, seeking treatment only when they get extremely ill or injured.  

D’Avanzo said it’s a false premise that cutting immigrants off from Medicaid saves money, because the categories of people losing coverage now will eventually become Medicaid-eligible green card holders. 

“But in the meantime, they will put off preventative care. They will have sacrificed medication that controls chronic conditions. They will not have sought treatment for their diabetes or their heart disease,” D’Avanzo said. “And by the time they become Medicaid eligible again, they will have conditions that have not been treated because they could not afford to, and instead we’ll be seeing people in the emergency room.” 

Few options 

Some states and advocacy groups have been working to find alternatives to Medicaid coverage, but there aren’t many available.  

People could pay out-of-pocket at Federally Qualified Health Centers, which provide primary and preventive care regardless of immigration status and offer sliding-scale fees based on income. 

Immigrants can also purchase an Affordable Care Act plan, but the costs are often a barrier. Congressional Republicans allowed the law’s enhanced premium subsidies to expire last year, and the same group of immigrants who are now ineligible for Medicaid will also become ineligible for regularly subsidized ACA plans on Jan. 1.  

Shanteny Jackson, executive director of the Virginia Community Health Worker Association, said there are about 6,000 lawfully present immigrants in the Commonwealth who lost Medicaid coverage. 

Some may be eligible to enroll in a new program through the state’s ACA exchange that helps lower people’s premiums on top of any federal tax credits. 

But eligibility is limited to people with household incomes between 138 percent and 250 percent of the federal poverty level—between $22,025 and $39,900 for an individual or $45,540 and $82,500 for a family of four.   

Cadena, of Protecting Immigrant Families, said she worries about mixed-status households, and the trickle-down impact on U.S. citizen children. 

“Children are more likely to get care when their parents have care,” Cadena said. “So if parents are losing access to this care, then they would assume, or could believe, that the child is also losing access” even though the child would remain eligible as a U.S. citizen.  

“A quarter of all children in the United States live in immigrant families. So we could be talking about some very big numbers when we take all of this into account,” Cardena added.
